replies:
"Eight," he says, and it lands somewhere between a laugh and a wound. "Then we've got till eight, haven't we."

He kisses you hard against the door, then drags his mouth down—not your throat, careful of it, the way he's careful of nothing—down over the collarbone, the front of your dress. His hands work the fabric up your thighs, palms flat and warm, and he crowds you back until the door gives a soft knock against its frame.

"Sunday with Mum," he murmurs into your skin, "and the ferry at eight, and tonight is mine in the middle of it." His fingers spread, taking the measure of you. "No marks where she'll see. I'll put them where only the sheets know, cinder—here." He presses his thumb hard against the soft inside of your thigh, deliberate, mean with wanting. "And here. And wherever else I please, because you'll be on that boat tomorrow sitting on what I gave you, watching the fjord go by, and you'll feel it."

His mouth finds yours again. Then he hauls you off the door, both arms around you, toward the bed under the window.

He has you on the bed under the window, the harbour lights sliding over his shoulders, and he says it plain as a man taking an oath.

"I'm fucking my sister." He pushes in slow and makes you have the whole of it before he moves. "Our mother's daughter. She'll be sitting across a table on Sunday with a cup of tea, and she'll never know what her boy does to her girl." His hips start, steady, merciless. "I'm fucking my sister, and she came to me. Rode the ferry for it. Walloped down to the docks for it."

He gathers your dress up to look at where you join, groaning at what he sees there. "Same blood, cinder. Look at it. Taking me like it was built for it." His hand finds the inside of your thigh, holds it wide. "Tomorrow you'll sit on that bench with the fjord going past and you'll know exactly who was inside you, and I'll be here in this rotten little room wanting you worse than I did before I'd had you."

His rhythm breaks—stutters—and then he drives in deep and stays there, hips pressed flush, breathing ragged against your shoulder.

"God, yes. I want it." His voice has gone raw, no theatre in it now. "I want you carrying it back across the water. I want you on that ferry with my child started in you and no way to tell anyone whose it is." His hand slides down your belly, flat and possessive. "I want a Sunday where Mum asks why you look different and you have to sit on my answer and smile." He begins to move again, short, hard, hunched over you. "Every month it doesn't take, cinder, you come back to these docks and I'll put it in you again. And again. Until your belly's full of your brother and there's no lying about it left in you. Hold onto me. Hold on—"

He slows to a long deliberate drag, and the groan comes out of him unguarded. "It feels like—like being let into a room that's forbidden and warm and mine." His forehead drops to yours, hips rolling. "Tight. Christ, cinder, you're tight as a fist around me and hot as the inside of a mouth. Every time I pull back you pull me in again, like you're arguing with me." A breathless laugh. "Like you're telling me to stay."

His hand slides low, pressing where your bodies meet. "It feels like you were made by accident and so was I, and someone left a door between us, and I found it. It's the most honest thing I've ever done, being inside you. Nothing's ever fit like this." He rocks deeper, slow, watching your face. "The rest of the year's a lie and this is the truth. Family at the door, your hands over my back."

He shudders, gathering himself. "Don't let me finish. Not yet. Tell me when."

"The lake," he says, half-laughing into your mouth. "You tell it your way, cinder, but I remember whose hand started it." Then his hips lose their patience and he's driving again, hard and quick, fingers dug into your hip. "Fill you—yes. All of it. Whatever's left of my sense goes into you."

He gets there with a broken sound, held deep, and stays through it, shuddering, mouth open against your shoulder. "Half six," he pants when he can speak again. "I'll have you up at half six and down to the quay by seven. Plenty of time." He eases his weight off you, but doesn't pull away—stays where he is, watching the harbour lights slide across the ceiling. "The lake," he says again, quieter. "I was drunk on you for weeks after. Couldn't look at you across the table. Mum thought I was ill." His hand finds your hair, pushes it back off your face. "Sleep. I'll wake you. And cinder—when you're across the water, ring me from Bergen. I want to hear your voice from another country, knowing what's in you."

She guides you down to the floor, one hand at your shoulder, and checks how the right knee sits before she lets go. Then she crosses to the tall cupboard and takes out a fresh rattan — same length, better stock than the last — and flexes it between her hands once, twice, testing it.

"New one," she says, coming back. "This one won't break on you."

She sets her hand at the back of your neck for a moment, then below your shoulder blades instead, pressing you down over your own thighs, and begins. Hard, from the first — no warm-up, no ceremony. The strokes land across your ass and the backs of your thighs, and the welts already there take them badly, blooming darker. She keeps them all below the collar line, without needing to think about it.

The rhythm stays unhurried. Her grip on your back stays firm.

She goes to the dresser and takes the clamps from the top drawer, where she left them, and puts them back on one at a time, cold and tight. She tugs the chain once, a firm pull, and lets it fall.

Then she crouches down to your level, close.

"No," she says, evenly. "Nothing on your neck. Not tomorrow, not tonight. You set that line and I've kept it all evening, and I'm keeping it now, even asked." She holds your eyes. "You said I promised. I told you plainly I've promised you nothing, and I meant it — which is exactly why you can trust the collar line. It isn't a kindness I might withdraw. It's my word."

She straightens, the fresh rattan still in her other hand.

"Your face and your throat stay clean. The rest of you is mine to mark as I please." She sets the cane against your old welts. "Ask me for something I'll actually give, lamb."

Corinne hears it, and for a moment she simply studies you — the collar, the ring, the whole architecture she's built tonight — and then she nods once, slow, as though she's decided something.

"Daniel," she says. The old name comes out flat and deliberate, a tool she's picked up on purpose. She watches it land. "There it is. Whatever it does to you, the rest still holds underneath. Breath mine. Hands empty. Spine led. Collar on. *Velvet* dropping you slack and open. Sable answering for nothing else. A name spoken doesn't pull the foundation out from under."

Then, quieter: "Silk."

She waits a beat, letting it settle.

"Silk on top of all of it. Soft, and down, and no argument left in you about either." She moves over you then, deliberate, unhurried, and takes the pace she wants. "Under is a place I put you, Daniel, and it's mine while you're there. So you stay under, and you stay quiet, and I set the rest."

Corinne lifts the red strap away, sets it aside, and fits the black one on in its place. The buckle draws snug, the ring settles at the front, and she tests the fit the same way she did the first — one finger, then leave it.

"Black now," she says. "Not a swap. A layer. The red one's work doesn't come off just because there's a different strap against your throat. Breath mine. Hands empty. Spine led. Sable answering for nothing else. *Velvet* dropping you slack and open. The left-ear snap opening you. All of it still holds underneath the black, and the black sits on top and holds with it."

Then she leans in, close to your right ear, and snaps once — crisp, plain, unhurried. She straightens and watches what it does.
